subject: chemistry_2
question_text: Calculate the molality of 2.5 g of ethanoic acid (CH₃COOH) in 75 g of benzene.

verification.note: From the boxed 'Problems : In text Questions' section of the chemistry half of "FAST TRACK IPE for Sr. Students", book p.68 (problem 3). A PROBLEM belongs to no printed paper section and the book prints no mark scheme for it, so both the Section-A placement and the 1+1 split are authored CLAIMS. Placed at 2 marks as a single-formula calculation, matching the Very Short Answer numericals this book already asks in the same unit. Neither the two-book union check nor a board back-test was possible for Chemistry-II: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is physics-only and first-year, and no second-year chemistry paper is in the corpus. Arithmetic re-derived independently and it agrees with the book: 2.5/60 = 0.04167 mol and 0.04167/0.075 = 0.5556 mol kg⁻¹. BOOK TYPO: the printed working spells the solvent 'banzene' once.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Moles of ethanoic acid
steps.why: Molality counts the moles of solute, so the 2.5 g must be divided by the molar mass first. Writing ethanoic acid as C₂H₄O₂ makes the count of each element plain, which is the safest way to reach 60 g mol⁻¹ without missing the second oxygen.
common_mistakes: Counting only one oxygen. The carboxyl group carries two, so the molar mass is 60, not 44.
Using the mass of benzene here. The solute is the ethanoic acid; the benzene belongs in the next step.
steps.memory_tip: Write CH₃COOH as C₂H₄O₂ before counting: 24 + 4 + 32 = 60.
steps.margin_note: Show the molar mass as a sum of the three element totals.

steps.label: The molality
steps.mark_note: Mass of solvent in kg and the value

lines.text: molality = moles of solute / kg of SOLVENT

steps.why: Molality divides by the mass of SOLVENT, not by the mass or volume of solution, which is the single fact that separates it from molarity. Because it uses a mass and not a volume, molality does not change with temperature, and that is why it is the concentration used in the boiling-point and freezing-point equations.
common_mistakes: Dividing by the total mass, 77.5 g. Molality uses the solvent alone.
Dividing by 75 instead of 0.075. Molality is per KILOGRAM of solvent.
Writing the unit as mol L⁻¹. That is molarity; molality is mol kg⁻¹.
steps.memory_tip: MolaLity uses the Litre-free mass of solvent in kg. MolaRity uses the volume of solution.
steps.margin_note: Convert grams to kilograms on its own line, and write the unit mol kg⁻¹.

insider_note: The mark is lost on the denominator far more often than on the molar mass: molality divides by the SOLVENT in kilograms, so it is 0.075 kg, not 75 g and not the 77.5 g of solution.
